query: A Cloudy Appointment {Tonight's appointment, says this morning's note, will go ahead "whatever the sky thinks". The sky thinks clouds, wall to wall.|Another clouded appointment tonight. The note is unbothered. "Starlight comes through cloud. It simply has to want to."|Cloud again tonight. You know the dome's cold corners and which way the gaps will drift.} {Somewhere behind the murk, the star you know best will be up.|The note says a thin gap may open in the west.|{season == "winter": It will be snow-cloud, heavy and low; your breath will freeze on the rail.|It will be warm cloud, with rain coming.}} Call through the cloud {The starlight comes down through the cloud like a rope through water, slow and then all at once. Your palms glow till dawn.|You call, and the cloud thins over your hands alone, a little round window in the sky. The lecturer writes for a long time.|You call the star by name and it answers, cloud or no cloud. You walk back down the stairs with light still in your fingers.} {You call until your hands shake. The cloud doesn't care. You go to bed drained and dark.|A thread of light comes halfway and frays in the murk. It takes something out of you as it goes.|You reach up for an hour into nothing. The lecturer says even nothing is a lesson. It doesn't feel like one.} Chart the gaps in the cloud {You sit by the rail all night logging the gaps, when and where and which stars peeked through. Cold to the bone; good data.|You chart the drift of the cloud like a sailor and predict the next gap to the minute. It comes; you're too frozen to cheer.|Your cloud log is pages long now. You know the sky's habits even when you can't see it, and your chest aches with cold.}
